newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: INTERVIEW - Liberty SAfrica units steam ahead.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Liberty SAfrica units steam ahead.

text.p: Liberty Life, the South African life insurance and financial services giant, said on Tuesday local operations were expected to steal the limelight this year following a strong performance from offshore in 1996.

Donald Gordon, chairman of the group with assets worth almost 120 billion rand (US$27 billion) excluding associates, told Reuters in an interview he expected a more robust showing from South African financial markets in 1997.

"Our local operations were affected by the very lacklustre markets last year so we didn't bring all that much of our capital gain through the accounts...but this year it seems to be looking much better," Gordon told Reuters late on Monday.

"The London results were very helpful to us (last) year and this time it could be the other way round. However, we are expecting great things from the U.K especially a continuation of our shopping centre success."

Gordon said some of Liberty's major stock investments had picked up substantially since last year when the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) had been hobbled by the meltdown in the rand, which lost 29 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar last year and nearly 40 percent against the British pound.
But in the first 2-1/2 months of this year the rand has managed to claw back some of its losses, helping the share market to appreciate strongly and bond yields to rally.
"So its looking good, although things can change," Gordon said.

Liberty Life, which boasts a market capitalisation of over 31 billion rand making it the fourth biggest firm on the JSE, last week released a strong batch of annual results showing a 27.8 percent surge in bottom line earnings for shareholders.

Offshore units, mainly consisting of U.K shopping centre properties housed in Liberty International Holdings, were a major contributor having taken advantage of a buoyant U.K. economy and the rand's devaulation against the pound.

Gordon said the recent appointment of former JSE president Roy Andersen as Liberty Life's chief executive elect would bring in "new blood" and raise the potential of the group which targets growth of 20 percent each year, but has consistently achieved over 25 percent over the past decade.
Gordon said he plans to stay at the helm for a "couple of years yet" -- he has not yet contemplated a retirement date -- acting as Andersen's mentor to ensure a smooth leadership transition.
"Obviously its going to take him some time to absorb all the nuances of the job, the tradition and the complexity of the companies and relationships," Gordon said.
Although insurance remains the core business of Liberty Life, Gordon said he was upbeat about the prospects for the group's U.K shopping developments.
"Shopping centres were the fundamental in the explosive growth of Liberty in the 1970s in South Africa. This will hopefully be replicated in the United Kingdom at some point in the future."
Another area of expected strong growth for the group over the next few years is the pension fund industry, Gordon said.

"It is going to be the biggest business and social sensitivity around the world in the next millenium to establish sufficient retirements funds so that the broad population can retire, not in poverty but with some expectation of a reasonable life post retirement."
He said no country in the world had made adequate retirement provision, at best providing 20 percent of the required funding.
"Some of the leading nations of the world including France and Germany are well below 10 percent on this criteria," he said.
